transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-25
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Lena Zhou (Mosaic VP Eng), Tom Barrett (Lead Backend), Sara Klein (DevOps)

Summary: Quick SDK integration walkthrough focused on Python and TypeScript quickstarts, auth patterns (API keys and SSO/SCIM question), env setup, and a path to a short POC. Customer interested in Dedicated pools for predictable latency; asked about SOC2/KMS and private networking options. Next steps captured at end.

Topics: SDK quickstarts, auth (API keys vs SSO/SAML), env vars and region selection, model selection and runtime, sample code and repo links, benchmark requirements, Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do about 45-60 minutes, ... a little walkthrough of the SDKs, quickstart, and then Diego will jump into some config and infra notes.
[00:22] Lena: Thanks Maya, excited. Real quick context: we handle checkout flows and post-purchase recs, mostly node services with a python ML microservice for chunking. Latency under 120ms preferred for completions at the edge.
[00:38] Diego: Awesome, that helps. We'll show both python and typescript snippets, auth patterns, and then touch Dedicated capacity since you mentioned predictable SLAs.
[00:48] Tom: For us, the auth question is big. We need SSO/SAML for console and API key rotation + KMS integration for customer data.
[01:15] Maya: Yes, we support API keys for service-to-service calls and enterprise SSO for Console access. For customer-managed keys we integrate with common KMS/HSM, and we have SOC 2 docs — I'll share.
[01:34] Sara: Do you support VPC peering or private link? Our infra team requires private connectivity for PII scopes.
[01:50] Diego: Yep, Redwood Private supports VPC/on-prem deployments and VPC peering. For hosted we also have region routing and private endpoints for certain enterprise tiers. I'll put links in the follow-up.
[02:10] Maya: Ok jumping into the SDK quickstart. First, python: pip install redwood-inference (note: transcriber may have typed package name slightly different). The quickstart sets REDWOOD_API_KEY and REDWOOD_API_BASE as env vars. Example: export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-xxx and export REDWOOD_API_BASE=https://api.redwood.ai.
[02:40] Diego: Right, code sample: from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'), base_url=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_BASE')); resp = client.generate(model='redwood-1.3', prompt='Hello'). The SDK handles streaming and retries.
[03:05] Lena: Do you have a typescript example? Our main app uses node.
[03:18] Diego: Yes. npm i @redwoodlabs/sdk (note: package name in the docs is @redwood-sdk, there was a short typo), then: import Redwood from '@redwoodlabs/sdk'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY, baseUrl: process.env.REDWOOD_API_BASE }); const res = await client.generate({ model: 'redwood-1.3', input: '...' });
[03:45] Tom: How do we handle environment separation for staging/prod? Config best practices?
[04:00] Maya: Use separate API keys per environment, separate projects in the Console, and pin model versions for reproducibility. We recommend using the Console to create keys with scoped permissions and expiration.
[04:18] Diego: Also enable token-level logging to trace requests per key in case of incidents; Console has RBAC so you can limit who can create keys.
[04:34] Sara: About model versions — if we pin a model, do you support gradual rollouts?
[04:45] Diego: Yes, rollouts/canary deploys are supported in Dedicated and Private. You can route a percentage of traffic to a new variant. I should note, the orchestration may fallback to smaller model variants on saturation — we call these compatible variants.
[05:10] Maya: We'll jump to auth deeper: for service calls, API keys are easiest. For interactive human access to the Console, SSO via SAML/Okta is supported. For provisioning we can do SCIM for user sync.
[05:35] Lena: Are audit logs available? We need long retention for compliance.
[05:45] Diego: Yes, audit logs and request logs can be shipped to your SIEM or stored in the Console depending on your plan — Dedicated/Private can offer longer retention.
[06:05] Maya: Quicknote on KMS: we support customer-managed keys; you'll need an integration step and validation as part of onboarding.
[06:20] Tom: Cool. Now on the SDK we want examples for streaming completions and function-calls.
[06:32] Diego: Streaming is supported. For python you can use client.stream_generate(...). For function calling we have structured output helpers; we'll send the sample repo which has both python and TS examples. Repo link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-examples (transcription may show slight repo path differences).
[07:00] Maya: Encouraging to run a local quickstart: we have a one-command demo: curl -sSL https://redwood.ai/quickstart | bash (this will scaffold examples), or check the Console quickstart pokes.
[07:20] Lena: For the POC, we'll want load profiles and throughput tests. What does the benchmark spreadsheet look like?
[07:33] Diego: We have a benchmark template showing tokens/request, concurrency, and cost estimates per-1000-tokens. I'll share the spreadsheet; it also maps to recommended instance types and quantization profiles.
[07:50] Tom: On the topic of Dedicated vs Hosted, can you summarize tradeoffs again?
[08:00] Maya: Sure — Hosted is fastest to start, usage-based pricing, good for early stages. Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools, predictable throughput, and isolation. Private adds VPC/on-prem and customer-managed keys and audit controls. For strict latencies and predictable budget, Dedicated is common.
[08:30] Sara: Does Dedicated require a long-term commit?
[08:36] Maya: Typically a monthly or annual reserved capacity contract, yes — but we can do trial bursts for POC.
[08:50] Diego: Quick note: when you measure latency, consider cold-starts vs warmed KV cache; our runtime uses continuous batching and KV cache to reduce per-token cost but first time paths can be higher.
[09:10] Lena: Ok thanks. Now environment variables — any gotchas for containers?
[09:20] Diego: Use secret stores (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager), avoid baking keys into images. The SDK supports standard env var names: REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_API_BASE, REDWOOD_REGION. If you're on Dedicated, the base_url will be zone-specific.
[09:45] Tom: Are there client-side connectors for feature flags or observability?
[09:52] Maya: We have libraries and hooks for OpenTelemetry tracing; the Console ingests traces and maps them to model routes. Also token-level cost metrics show up in the Console.
[10:10] Lena: Example of a minimal python quickstart?
[10:18] Diego: Sure: 1) pip install redwood-inference 2) export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-xxx 3) python -c "from redwood import Client; c=Client(); print(c.generate('hi'))" — again, tiny transcription issues maybe in the import path but repo has exact snippet.
[10:44] Sara: Typescript minimal?
[10:48] Diego: npm init -y; npm i @redwoodlabs/sdk; create index.mjs with import Redwood from '@redwoodlabs/sdk'; const c = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); console.log(await c.generate({ input: 'hi' }));
[11:08] Tom: How do we run integration tests in CI without exposing keys?
[11:15] Maya: Use ephemeral API keys with limited scopes and rotate them during the test. We can also provide a test project for POC so you don't use prod keys.
[11:33] Lena: Good. Security review questions: can we get SOC2, architecture diagrams, penetration test results?
[11:42] Maya: We'll attach the security whitepaper and SOC2 report in follow-up. For pen tests we provide summaries and we can coordinate an NDA if you want more detail.
[11:58] Diego: For data in flight and at rest we use TLS, and for customer-managed keys the ciphertext handling is described in the KMS doc.
[12:10] Maya: I'll add the security docs link in the notes.
[12:20] Tom: One more infra question: do you stream logs to S3 or SIEM?
[12:26] Diego: Both supported — we can push request logs to your S3, or ship to Splunk/Datadog.
[12:36] Lena: Thanks. Let's look at an example of a function-call pattern and structured outputs.
[12:44] Diego: Sure — the SDK has a functions schema helper; you can pass a JSON schema for structured outputs and the SDK will coerce responses, including type hints. There's an example in the repo under experiments/functions.
[13:10] Maya: Quick demo: I'll share my screen and run the typescript sample to show live stream — (screen share) ... buffering a little, small hiccup, seems ok, streaming chunks coming in.
[13:45] Maya: You can see the partial tokens and the SDK's event hooks for progress.
[14:02] Tom: Nice. What about cost controls?
[14:10] Diego: We provide per-route quotas and token limits, and suggestions from Redwood Optimize for batching, caching, and quantization to meet cost targets. We'll include Optimize recommendations in the POC spreadsheet.
[14:36] Lena: For quantization, do you recommend int8 for our workloads?
[14:44] Diego: Depends on model and accuracy needs; we can recommend quant profiles based on your quality tests — Optimize produces candidate profiles.
[15:00] Maya: Ok wrapping up main demo. Recap of next steps: Maya shares pricing & security docs; Diego shares benchmark template and sample infra; schedule POC kickoff week of 7/6. We'll give you a test project and repo links.
[15:20] Lena: Sounds good. A few closing clarifications: can we get a sample Terraform?
[15:29] Diego: Yes, sample Terraform and helm charts are in the infra folder of the repo. I'll send those.
[15:40] Sara: Also can you include a small checklist for the onboarding runbook?
[15:46] Maya: Yep, we'll include runbook: keys, VPC peering request, KMS setup, audit log retention config.
[15:56] Tom: Great. Thank you both.
[16:00] Maya: Thanks everyone — I'll follow up with the links.

References and Links Mentioned:
- SDK repo (example): https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-examples
- Quickstart: https://redwood.ai/quickstart
- Security whitepaper & SOC2 (to be attached)
- Benchmark template (to be shared)

End of transcript.
